turns.replyText:
Can you explain the main options in simple terms?

Absolutely, I can break it down simply.

Think of your choices in three big buckets:

What kind of rose shape you want
Shrub/bush roses: Round, bushy plants that give lots of blooms. Great for most gardens and beginners.
Climbing roses: Long canes you tie to an arch, fence, trellis, or wall. Beautiful for entrances and pergolas but need some structure to grow on.
Groundcover/landscape roses: Low and spreading, good for covering a slope or the front of a border.
Hybrid tea roses (classic long-stem): Tall, with one big bloom per stem. These are the “florist-style” roses people often cut for vases.
How you’ll use it
Showpiece near a door or path: A shrub or hybrid tea rose works well.
Covering a fence or arch: Choose a climbing rose.
Filling a bed with color and less shaping: Shrub or groundcover roses.
Cutting flowers for vases: Hybrid teas and some shrub roses that make long stems.
Whether it fits your conditions
Sunlight: Roses like full sun (at least 6 hours of direct sun per day). If a plant says “partial shade,” it can manage with about 4+ hours.
Hardiness zone: This is how cold your winters get. On our site you can select your zone at the top so you only see roses that will live in your climate.

How our roses arrive

All our roses are own-root roses in 1-gallon containers with soil. They arrive trimmed back and without leaves so they travel safely. You plant them in the ground (or a larger pot) and they leaf out and grow once settled in.

turns.replyText:
Is there anything else a beginner needs to get started?

You’re asking all the right questions. Let’s keep it simple so you can actually get started without feeling overwhelmed.

Here’s what most beginners really need beyond the rose itself:

A decent planting spot
Full sun: Aim for at least 6 hours of direct sun.
Well‑draining soil: Water should not sit around the roots for long.
Basic tools
A shovel or trowel
Gardening gloves
A watering can or hose with a gentle spray
Optional but very helpful: soil amendments These improve the soil your rose will live in. They’re not required, but they give your plant a nice head start.
Bone meal: Supports strong root development when you plant.
Cow manure: Adds long‑term nutrients and organic matter to the soil.
Mint compost: Loosens heavy soil and can be used mixed into the planting area or as a top layer to protect roots.
Worm castings: Gentle, slow nutrients and better soil structure.

You can absolutely plant without these, but using one or two (especially compost or manure plus bone meal) usually helps roses establish faster.

Something to feed the rose (fertilizer) Fertilizing is important for good growth and blooms.
We offer options like OmniMeal and Founders Fish Fertilizer, but you can use any quality rose or balanced garden fertilizer.
For the first year, a liquid fertilizer is easiest for beginners because it’s simple to mix with water and gentle when used as directed.
You’ll follow the directions on the fertilizer label for how often to feed.
Mulch (very nice to have)
A 2–3 inch layer of mulch around (but not touching) the base of the rose helps keep moisture in and moderates soil temperature.

If you’d like, I can walk you step‑by‑step through exactly how to plant your first rose using just the basics (rose, shovel, water, and maybe one or two of the amendments above). Just tell me if you’re planning to plant in the ground or in a large container outdoors.

turns.replyText:
How do I use it properly the very first time?

Love that you’re thinking ahead about doing it right the first time.

Because timing and a few details depend on where you live, I’ll give you a simple starter checklist and then ask a couple quick questions.

Here’s how to “use” your first rose properly when it arrives:

Unpack and water
Take the rose out of the box the day it arrives.
Set it outdoors in a bright spot (not hot, blazing sun the first day).
Water slowly until water runs out the bottom of the pot.
Check if it’s the right time to plant Roses should go in the ground only:
After your last spring frost, or
At least 6 weeks before your first fall frost.

If it’s not in that window, you’ll keep it in a larger outdoor container for a while instead of planting in the ground right away.

Planting basics (ground or container)
Choose a spot with full sun (6+ hours of direct sun daily).
Dig a hole about 2 feet wide and 2 feet deep if going in the ground, or use a large container (about 10–15 gallons) if you’re growing it in a pot.
Mix some compost or aged manure into your soil if you have it; if not, just use your existing soil.
Set the rose so the soil level in the pot is even with the surrounding soil, not buried deeper.
Backfill, press gently to remove air pockets, and water deeply.
Add a 2–3 inch layer of mulch around (but not touching) the base to keep moisture in.
First-season care
Keep the soil evenly moist (not soggy) while it’s getting established.
Once you see 4–6 inches of new growth, you can start a gentle liquid fertilizer according to the label.

Two important points about our roses:

They are own-root roses in 1-gallon containers with soil (not bare root), so you’ll be planting a potted plant.
They must live outdoors; keeping them indoors long term will cause problems and also voids our guarantee.
